data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Network topology determines correlated failure resilience: a decentralized network reduces correlated failure risk only if it is organized as a modular, loosely-coupled directed acyclic graph (DAG); a large centralized service is strictly more resilient if it avoids acyclic dependency graphs that allow cascading failures.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decentralized network organically evolves into a hub-and-spoke topology for efficiency, it loses its topological advantage and becomes functionally centralized.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service strictly enforces bulkheading and circuit breakers between its internal redundant components, it achieves the same failure isolation as the decentralized DAG without the operational overhead.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Correlated failures in complex systems often manifest as cascading failures where the failure of one node increases the load or probability of failure on its dependencies. A decentralized network of independent services naturally enforces loose coupling and limits blast radius. If the topology forms a DAG, upstream failures do not automatically propagate to all downstream nodes because alternative paths or buffered isolation exist. In contrast, a large service with 'strictly more total internal redundancy' often scales by tightly coupling components, creating hidden cycles or critical shared busses that synchronously fail under load.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
